title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
description: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcemen
body: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.""We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added. "We will update the public when more information is available."The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.The information was put in a database named Icepick.Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE. Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.   The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets."The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the groups work to hack DHS records. "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security. The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents. In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt. Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people. Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement. Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

schema.headline: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack

title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
description: If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.S
body: If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

schema.headline: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?

title: George Michael: Family row over dozens items up for auction
description: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the F
body: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.  Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will. Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin. In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories."I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said."She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".It has an estimated price tag of between £60,000 and £120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to £600 and a current bid of £1,750.Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music."I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart"."I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

schema.headline: George Michael: Family row over dozens items up for auction

title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
description: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had
body: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people. Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus. The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap. The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.  The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladderThe scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

schema.headline: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
description: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Sev
body: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened."I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described."I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms.""It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms."She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims."The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."Most political parties in Spain cancelled their campaign events scheduled for Wednesday.The exception was the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence."Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party."If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.

schema.headline: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain

title: What we now know about the UK economy in four charts
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichael RaceBusiness reporterThe UK may have no involvement in the US-Iran war, but the country is feeling the full force
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichael RaceBusiness reporterThe UK may have no involvement in the US-Iran war, but the country is feeling the full force of the conflict on its economy.Soaring energy prices are set to dent growth in the short term, push up inflation and leave living standards in a "grim" place, according to the latest official forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).Interest rates are also predicted to rise, making borrowing more expensive, along with government debt repayments.Chancellor John Healey warned the nation faces "real challenges ahead" as he announced policies that he said would offer "breathing space" for households in the coming months."What we face today are global economic storms," he said. "We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them."In its first assessment of the UK economy since the Middle East conflict started, the OBR said rising energy prices were the biggest risk to the economy in the near future.Despite raising its growth forecast for this year, it sharply cut its prediction for next year from 1.6% to 1%.Growth is then set to rebound in the following years.When an economy grows, businesses tend to invest more, create more jobs and give pay rises to workers, which leaves people feeling better off on average, though it can take time and not everyone necessarily benefits.Companies making higher profits also pay more in tax, which can enable the government to spend more on public services. When there is slow economic growth, or the economy shrinks, the opposite can occur.Inflation can weigh on growth and the OBR has forecast that prices are set to rise at a faster pace as higher energy bills filter through supply chains and to consumers, especially in 2027.High global oil prices have already hit drivers at the pumps, with petrol priced at almost £1.73 per litre on average, while diesel is near £1.99.Elevated oil prices over time can lead to prices edging upwards across a host of goods, such as food, as companies pass on the higher expenses they face to consumers.Goods are typically transported to destinations by lorries and vans, so high fuel prices can have far-reaching consequences.The OBR now thinks inflation will stay higher for longer than previously forecast, peaking at 3.8% in 2027.Despite the cost-of-living support announced by the government, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics said the measures were "small beer given the surge in inflation we expect over the winter".High inflation paints a bleak picture when it comes to living standards and the OBR has forecast a dip next year as energy bills hit the spending power of households. Those on lower incomes are set to be hit harder, however, because energy costs eat up a bigger share of their monthly budget and disposable income.Real household disposable income, a measure of living standards, is forecast to grow from 2027, but not by as much as previously thought."It's a pretty grim picture," according to the OBR's David Miles, who says there has been "virtually no growth" for individuals since before the Covid pandemic."It's been a dismal period in British economic history."Inflation is expected to average 3.4% next year, before falling to the Bank of England's 2% target towards the end of the decade.The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates next week due to higher inflation in recent months. Rates are currently at 3.75%, but the OBR now forecasts they could rise to as high as 4.5% in the coming years.It had previously forecast two interest rate cuts this year.Higher rates makes borrowing money more expensive but can boost returns on savings.Inflation also raises the cost of borrowing for the government, with spending on debt interest set to rise.Such repayments are also predicted to increase the overall amount the government borrows, which is set to increase every year by more than had been previously forecast by the OBR.Higher spending on welfare and pensions due to inflation is also expected to increase borrowing, though it is forecast to fall as a share of the economy over the next five years.However, forecasts are only a best guess at what might happen in the future. Given the way the conflict in the Middle East has upended previous predictions, the future of the war could alter inflation expectations.US President Donald Trump has suggested the war will end after the mid-term elections next month. The OBR admitted there remained "significant uncertainty" around its predictions due to the changing situation in the Middle East.

schema.headline: What we now know about the UK economy in four charts

title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
description: Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site w
body: Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists."We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council."We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselves… we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes. The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee. The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.The King ended his day with a garden reception at Government House in Nassau where he met Bahamians who have made significant contributions to public life.In a speech, Dame Cynthia A Pratt, the governor general of the Bahamas who is the King's representative on the island, described her pride at Charles visiting the country for the first time since 1973."We trust that your time in our capital will reflect the legendary hospitality of our people," said Dame Cynthia."We pray that this royal visit further strengthens the enduring bonds of friendship between the Crown and the Bahamian people."On Thursday, the Caribbean tour leaves the Bahamas as the King continues his visit in Guyana.The trip has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.The King's engagements in Guyana will focus on the environment and biodiversity.He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

schema.headline: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour

title: Neighbours: AI micro-drama recut of Australian show focusing on Margot Robbie worries actors and crew
description: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.Fr
body: Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed. Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman."It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature."If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article."I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said."AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it"."We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks."Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

schema.headline: Neighbours: AI micro-drama recut of Australian show focusing on Margot Robbie worries actors and crew

title: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions
description: "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons i
body: "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in 1947.His aphorism came to mind as Israel's election results filtered through on Tuesday night - exit polls blending with ballots that were cast to dash or fulfil people's hopes and fears.This election has, in some ways, been a celebration of democracy. Voters turning out in record numbers, Jews and Arabs alike. Many spent thousands to fly in from abroad to cast their ballot.At polling stations across the country, we saw the passion of campaigners, as they used every minute to try to change that last mind and win that last vote.President Isaac Herzog said the election was a "badge of honour" for Israeli society. "It is remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he exclaimed.Yet this election left the most established democracy in the Middle East without a clear path to a new government. It produced an inconclusive result where neither opposing bloc will have a majority in parliament.Some might say this was business as usual. Israel has never had a one-party government. Its fragmented, proportional representation system is almost designed to govern by coalition.Yet many commentators warned this election had revealed the fundamental and perhaps growing divisions that scar this nation. This was not a plebiscite in which an electorate united around a single cause.How these vastly diverging views coalesce into some form of government is now the unenviable task facing Israel's body politic - the choices and compromises they may have to make could involve fundamental decisions about the country's future.Would Netanyahu be ready to abandon his religious allies and form a coalition with right-wingers from the opposition bloc? Would they be ready to swallow their hostility towards the prime minister and sit in his government?Is the opposition bloc ready to abandon much of its campaign promises and co-operate with Arab parties to force Netanyahu out of office? Are the Arab parties ready to risk joining a government that could fall within months?Yair Golan, the left-wing Democrat leader, urged the opposition bloc to form a partnership with Arab parties. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said.But are the people of Israel ready for such a reality? Amit Segal, an Israeli commentator sympathetic towards Netanyahu, said the high turnout among Arab Israeli voters "reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all".The risk is that this election, instead of putting Israel on a new path, has instead raised further doubts about what it is that unites its citizens. What are the common factors that bind this complex, varied collection of peoples into one polity?Autocratic governments, which are growing in number, have long criticised democracies for producing weak and temporary governments, often fragile coalitions that struggle to hold together, let alone deliver what the people wanted.Israel may now struggle for months to form a government. It might even fail and have to hold another election. President Herzog acknowledged this risk head on as he prepared to open coalition negotiations: "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections."For years, Israel has focused on defending itself against its external enemies. But must it also now be ready to defend itself from perils within, if the divisions writ large by this election become unmanageable?In another speech, Churchill once said democracy was not just "insurance against dangers from abroad". It was also, he added, "insurance against dangers scarcely less grave and much more near and constant which threaten us here at home".Can Israel's democracy live up to this challenge?

schema.headline: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions

title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
description: Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenko
body: Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc."The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority"."We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results."I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.Mahdi Kabaha who lives in a village near Haifa and campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic"."Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition."We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it."The opposition parties cannot dictate any conditions," Jabareen said. "If the opposition in Israel are willing to afford real and substantive change, and an alternative for the dangerous, extreme-right-wing government... they will have to negotiate with us."

schema.headline: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show

title: Red Roses: Ellie Kildunne named on bench for second England match in a row
description: Ellie Kildunne has been named on the England bench for their fixture against the USA, despite head coach John Mitchell making six changes to his side.
body: Ellie Kildunne has been named on the England bench for their fixture against the USA, despite head coach John Mitchell making six changes to his side. The 27-year-old full-back was dropped for the 31-22 defeat by Canada last Saturday, with Mitchell saying she needed to show "greater consistency".Despite the loss in Ottawa, Bristol Bears star Kildunne will once again have to settle for a place on the bench for Friday's match against the USA in New Jersey, with Emma Sing retaining her spot.With 67 England caps to her name, Kildunne was named World Rugby's player of the year in 2024, and starred in the Red Roses' 2025 World Cup victory. Four of Mitchell's changes are to the backs, with Tatyana Heard, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Flo Robinson and Holly Aitchison handed their first starts of the tour, while forwards Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir replace Hannah Botterman and Sarah Bern. "Our intent is to start this next phase strongly against the USA, with six months until our next Test in the Women's Six Nations," said Mitchell. "We're rotating some positions this week to refresh the group, create opportunities and continue building our depth."Selection is driven by what the team needs against the USA, the behaviours we value and the performance we're preparing to deliver."Everyone has a role, and everyone is accountable for our standards."

schema.headline: Red Roses: Ellie Kildunne named on bench for second England match in a row

title: Carabao Cup draw: Fleetwood Town to face Everton or Newcastle in quarter-final
description: League Two side Fleetwood Town will face Everton or Newcastle United at Highbury in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.The lowest-ranked side left
body: League Two side Fleetwood Town will face Everton or Newcastle United at Highbury in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.The lowest-ranked side left in the competition have already made history by reaching the last eight after they stunned Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties on Tuesday.They will have to wait to find out their next opponents, with Everton hosting Newcastle at Hill Dickinson Stadium in the final match of the fourth round on Thursday.Holders Manchester City will host the only other non-Premier League side - League One Bradford City - at Etihad Stadium after they needed penalties to get past Brighton in the last 16.The other two fixtures will be all-Premier League affairs with Liverpool, who also required a penalty shootout to beat Chelsea, hosting Bournemouth and Crystal Palace taking on Sunderland at Selhurst Park.Quarter-final fixtures will take place in the week commencing 14 December.

schema.headline: Carabao Cup draw: Fleetwood Town to face Everton or Newcastle in quarter-final

title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
description: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.The Heroe
body: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment."Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

schema.headline: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe

title: Estevao: Why is the Brazilian becoming Chelsea's forgotten man?
description: The last time Chelsea beat Liverpool, Estevao was the talk of the Premier League.The Brazilian was still in his first couple of months at Stamford Bri
body: The last time Chelsea beat Liverpool, Estevao was the talk of the Premier League.The Brazilian was still in his first couple of months at Stamford Bridge when his name hit the headlines after he scored the winner against the Premier League champions with practically the final kick of the match last October.Fast forward 12 months, and Estevao is beginning to attract attention for all the wrong reasons as he struggles to force his way into Xabi Alonso's side.The 19-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Palmeiras last summer, was conspicuous by his absence on Wednesday night as Chelsea were knocked out of the Carabao Cup following a penalty shootout loss to Liverpool at Anfield.The Blues had taken the lead in the first half through Morgan Rogers, but they failed to kick on after Cody Gakpo quickly restored parity for the hosts.Most concerning for Estevao, though, was that as both teams pushed for a winner in the second half, Alonso never appeared to consider the forward.The clearest indication of just how low Estevao sits in Alonso's pecking order came midway through the second half, when Alonso made a triple substitution in an attempt to turn the game in his side's favour.One of the three changes was Emanuel Emegha, who had yet to feature for the Blues since his summer move from Strasbourg.Just moments after that triple change, which brought Chelsea's total number of substitutions to five, Estevao could be seen ending his warm-up and retreating to the bench.It was another night of no action for the Brazilian.Sadly for Estevao, Wednesday night's situation at Anfield was nothing new for him.The Brazilian has failed to make the starting XI in any of the eight Premier League matches since Alonso took charge of the Blues in the summer.His total minutes for the campaign so far stand at an underwhelming 172, with 125 of those coming in the victories over Luton Town and Leeds United in the earlier rounds of the EFL Cup.Yet even in the thrilling 6-3 win against Daniel Farke's side, which remains one of only two games he has started this campaign, he was withdrawn at half-time with Chelsea trailing 1-0.After the fourth-round defeat by Liverpool, Alonso defended his decision not to play Estevao, hinting that the forward is still coming to grips with the physical demands of English football."We started with Pedro [Neto], Morgan [Rogers] and Danny Welbeck, and the game had very intense moments," said Alonso."We knew it was going to be physical, and Malo [Gusto] had cramps, so we were a bit forced with substitutions. The season is going to be very long, and there will be moments for everyone."When asked directly about the Brazilian, Alonso added: "He could be happier. He wants to play. I'm sure Estevao will have his moment, it is my responsibility."We know the game in England is really intense, and you need to be up for it. Estevao is in his second season. The season is going to be long."One of the main reasons behind Estevao's exile has been the form of Pedro Neto.It was only a couple of months ago that Portugal international Neto looked destined to leave Chelsea, only two years after joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers. The 26-year-old was linked with a move to Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, but he ultimately remained at Stamford Bridge.That decision appears to have been influenced by Alonso, who has underlined his faith in Neto by handing him seven starts in eight Premier League matches this season.His success out on the right - which also happens to be Estevao's favoured position - has meant opportunities have been few and far between for the Brazilian.He has primarily been deployed as a right-sided wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 system, with his Premier League experience and greater defensive solidity compared to Estevao seemingly winning over the Spaniard.After an impressive start to the campaign, in which he has scored four goals in 11 matches, Neto was rewarded with a new six-year deal at Stamford Bridge."He's a player who is a little bit of a victim of the system," former Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff told Sky Sports."Alonso tends to play Neto in that hybrid wing-back role, expecting him to get high up the pitch as well. Maybe he doesn't feel that suits Estevao, and I don't feel it does either."One area that has not been a problem for the Blues this season is attack, with the forward positions firmly in the hands of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Rogers, who has made a spectacular start to life at Stamford Bridge following his £117m move from Aston Villa.Against Liverpool, though, Estevao couldn't even get a look-in despite Chelsea being without the suspended Palmer and the injured Joao Pedro."How Estevao has not got on the pitch tonight, I do not know," said former Crystal Palace forward Clinton Morrison."He must be thinking, 'What do I have to do? We have injuries to two of the star players up front, and I'm still not getting on the pitch'."Estevao will be hoping he can follow in the footsteps of Neto and revive his Stamford Bridge career.

schema.headline: Estevao: Why is the Brazilian becoming Chelsea's forgotten man?

title: 'I live with a ghost': Japan's haunted homes attract bargain hunters
description: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a
body: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says."Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in."I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties."[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US. But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., externalBack in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.For support and more information on any of the topics raised in this article, help is available on the BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: 'I live with a ghost': Japan's haunted homes attract bargain hunters
